grades.quote: The addrs array records the block numbers of the disk blocks holding the file’s content.
grades.reason: Explains ordinary inode block-address storage, but not what happens when the addresses exceed its capacity.

grades.quote: represented as an _inode_ with a unique i-number and some blocks holding the file’s data.
grades.reason: Provides basic file-representation context but no mechanism for addresses that do not fit in the inode.
Discusses general block mapping and allocation, not inode capacity or overflow representations.

grades.quote: HFS Plus takes an approach quite reminiscent of traditional UNIX inodes: the first eight extent map entries are stored directly in the inode-like structure, whether they are the only ones or just the first few of a larger number. Any additional entries are stored elsewhere, in a single B<sup>+</sup> -tree that serves for all the files, as I will describe subsequently.
grades.reason: Directly explains how extent maps exceeding inode capacity are represented using external B+ trees, with HFS Plus and XFS examples.
